utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Madam Registrar, would you please be so kind as to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon Your Honours, good afternoon everybody in the courtroom. This is IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And since I do not see any new faces today in the courtroom, I think we can skip the normal introduction of appearances. So I will on that note proceed directly to welcoming everybody this afternoon and especially to you, Mr. Karavelic, and I have to remind you that you are still under oath and also that there is a severe punishment for giving false testimony or incorrect testimony. Madam Vidovic, I believe that you are just about to finish your examination in chief. You have 10 or 15 minutes left, if I consult with the registrar. I should be informed. Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Before that, Your Honour, I would note that instead of three judges there are only two today and I was wondering if you could maybe put that on the record that we're sitting under Rule 15 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Certainly. I was just coming to that. As you can see, Judge Moloto is away for the day and so we are sitting this afternoon pursuant to Rule 15 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The registrar informs me, Madam Vidovic, that you have only used five hours and three minutes which leaves you with another 57 minutes of examination in chief. I'm sorry for that mistake. Any other matters to raise before we can start? That is not the case. The floor is yours, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I believe I will conclude my examination even before that, as I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General Karavelic. I hope you've rested well and that we will conclude this questioning relatively soon. I'd like to show the witness Exhibit 1292, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know whether the problem I have is shared by everyone in the courtroom. I don't see the document in front of me. I see the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I apologise, Madam Vidovic, there is, it appears, a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: General Karavelic, do you see the document in front of you? It should bear the date of the 20th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to page 2 in B/C/S and the third page in the English version. Could we please see the bottom of the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, my question is this: We see the initials KV. Are these your initials and do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you draft the document? Did you author it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did that together with General Enver Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to page 1 of the document now. I wish to remind you that in your testimony yesterday, you said you saw General Delic upon his return from abroad in Zagreb. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is about an agreement between the top military figures in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. In Zagreb, in the presence of certain representatives of the International Community, there were meetings and talks held on joint operations and joint use of forces between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croatian Defence Council and the Croatian army in order to liberate western Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you the following: Who was present at those talks on behalf of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see from the document, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic was there, president of the Presidency, as well as the Supreme Commander and Mr. Delic as the commander of the general staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The date is 20 September, 1995. Do you remember how long did the military talks last with the military authorities of the Republic of Croatia, if you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were two meetings. One was political, the other one was military.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As regards this date, the 20th of September, 1995, what was the duration of the talks?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, a few days.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please assign an exhibit number to this document or rather it is an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a very short question for the witness. Sir, how is it that the document was not signed directly by the commander, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because he was attending another more important task. He wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but at the meeting, he was present, right? We have the report from the meeting and he was present, you say. So in the English version, could the correction be made in saying that the document was signed for Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for your correction. We will do that. Let us clarify something concerning Her Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke of the meeting that was held in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was referred to here is a document from Kakanj in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say he wasn't present, what did you want to say?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he was either in Zagreb or on a business trip or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did you mean that he wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After this meeting, where did you go, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you specifically or precisely as to what followed this meeting, but I too went to Zagreb in the course of the next few days in order to work on many military details that needed to be elaborated. Later on, I was busy implementing the order we have before us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the implementation of the order, did you go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Novi Travnik, my task was to organise a command post there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did combat activities follow?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When exactly?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but the combat activities began in late September or early October.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1995, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the area that the combat activities took place in?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking from the central part of Bosnia from the feature of Vlasic, it was to the north and to the south in the direction of Mrkonjic Grad, Jajce and Banja Luka. On the other side from the Bihac enclave, that is from the western side, there were combat activities from the River Sava in Bosanska Krupa all the way up to Bosanski Petrovac and Drvar. Combat activities developed towards the east, towards Kljuc, Sanski Most, Prijedor, and Banja Luka. From the south, combat was moving upwards from Livno and Glamoc towards Mrkonjic Grad and Mount Manjaca and further on to Banja Luka. It was a very large semicircle.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your thorough explanation. In the period that you mentioned, and you said it was late September and early October, were you visited by any military or political figures in the area of combat?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, that's a leading question and it would suggest the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond? I don't think this is a leading question. It is correct that one can answer with a yes or no to this question; however, it doesn't mean that such questions are always leading. This one cannot be leading because I asked him whether any military or political figures visited. The question in itself does not imply either or both of those groups. I don't see how this would be leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, I guess you could have asked whether they received any visits but be that as it may, I will allow you to continue with the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It would not have been specific enough. The witness might believe I was asking him about some journalists visiting or such.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, Witness, did you understand my question? Can you provide us an answer?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't remember seeing any senior political figures such as Mr. Izetbegovic at that moment. He did come at a later stage though, but there were many visits by officers of the General Staff including the commander, General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is difficult for me to tell you a date, but it was in October.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a few brief questions on this topic. Do you know how the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was ended?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the signing of the Dayton Peace Accords.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any peace talks preceding the signing of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the General Staff and its commander play a role in the talks?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a very large one. The commander of the General Staff played a role in the preparation of all elements needed to our political delegation to participate at the peace talks in Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To clarify another thing we discussed yesterday, in your yesterday's testimony, and now I go back to 1993, you mentioned communication means and packet communication, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that corps commanders had such communication with the General Staff at the time. How did the system work as regards the corps? Did you have such communication at your disposal with your subordinate units, can you explain briefly?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Packet communication --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I rise just because I object on the grounds that this is a compound question. When he gives his answer, it might not be clear which answer he's -- the question he's actually answering. If Madam Vidovic wants to put two questions to him, it would be best in terms of the record if she puts those separately rather than in the space of one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wood. If you can lead your witness through those two questions separately, it would be helpful. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank my colleague, Mr. Wood, for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, can you explain if you had packet communications with your subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Packet communications were available only to the General Staff when communicating with corps commands, with air defence and anti-aircraft defence, because it's the most expensive and the most complex system of communication. It requires computers, it requires optical visibility, a number of repeaters as well for all that to function. This is all very expensive and in the first years, we did not have any at all. We received our first resources of that kind somewhere in 1993, enough for the corps to have it. Now, communications were completely different from the corps down. There were no packet communications there and these communications are of vital importance between the corps and the divisions, divisions and brigades, brigades towards battalions, battalions towards companies, companies towards squads. There are 7 or 8 levels. The lower down you go in the chain, the greater number of devices you must have and packet communications were much too expensive for that. We had even brigades and even battalions without any communication devices at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you a few brief questions more. In the course of June 1993, were you involved in any combat activities in Central Bosnia such as the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you in any way whatsoever participate in the process of dealing with the Mujahedin problem in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks, because you just put your last question to the witness to which I may have a follow-up so I might as well put it now. My question was related to something that you told us a couple of days ago about your participation in a Council for Protection of the Constitutional Order. And if I'm not mistaken, you told us that you had frequently attended these meetings and that I think the events that brought these meetings up in this courtroom were the events that led to the fall of Caco and Celo, the commanders of the 9th and 10th Brigade and I think you told us that you were present at the council meeting for that purpose on that particular day. My question would be: Was the issue of the -- of possible disciplinary actions against the insubordination of the Mujahedin ever raised in that council, the Council for Protection of the Constitutional Order or the commission? I'm not sure about which is the correct expression but do you know what I'm talking about? So my question is: In that body, did you ever discuss ways in which to handle the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That body is called Council for the Protection of the Constitutional Order of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That council was headed by the Serb member of the Presidency of The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Mirko Pejanovic. I cannot tell you exactly how many times but at least twice I attended their meetings and I do not recall that we ever touched upon that subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Lattanzi has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only have one question. Witness, you've talked in detail yesterday about problems that the 1st Corps was experiencing in terms of control and you were the commander of that corps. I would like to know if you ever found out that some problems with regard to command and control also occurred in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really cannot tell you anything specific except that occasionally I heard some stories, hearsay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You talked about some stories, hearsay, did you ever hear, through this hearsay, that Commander Delic or General Delic, if you will, or that the Presidency as a whole or the presidents of the Presidency ever took any measures to take care of these issues with regard to the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, it's difficult to say anything precise because all the communications towards the 3rd Corps were totally independent of me, bypassed me completely; I was not involved in that communication. And all the meetings, especially in the first three years of the war, only took place in Sarajevo. I have knowledge that certain measures had been taken but it's very difficult for me to say which measures, to what extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were there any meetings of corps commanders where questions were debated with regard to the problems that all corps commanders had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the second half of 1994, and in 1995, we did sometimes have meetings among corps commanders, usually without the commander of the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the commander of the 3rd Corps was there, if I understand correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I don't know how many though, maybe two meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That commander never told you of any problems that occurred while they were commanding or while they were giving orders. Did they tell you about problems that they had in terms of getting obeyed by the subordinate units? It's just a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Really, no. I don't see why he would share his problems with me. I did not share mine with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what was discussed during those meetings if not of -- did you discuss common problems that all corps commanders had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Corps commanders would brief others about the overall current political and military situation, each for his own area of responsibility and at the end of these reports, the commander would give a summing up and issue assignments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But there were no questions of command and control of subordinate units? Did you never discuss that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. Yesterday, we looked at a document from a meeting in Zenica back in September, October 1993. Of course, the answer is yes, it was openly discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And at these meetings, was there ever a question of the fact that the 3rd Corps had problems in terms of having the Mujahedin unit obey them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we did. The corps commander would give a briefing, the superior commander would listen, and issue him an assignment. Meanwhile, I think about my own briefing and how to make it better. I was less concerned with problems in the 2nd and in the 5th Corps and the 3rd. I had too many problems of my own to give much thought to how other corps commanders would deal with their own. It was up to General Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Mr. Wood, are you ready to begin your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General Karavelic. As you might know by now, my name is Mr. Wood, Kyle Wood. I represent the Prosecution and you are an old hand at this, you know that I will be asking questions on behalf of the Prosecution. Now, you've told us, General, that you've testified in four previous trials. And I'll just read the dates of those and you can tell me whether or not this is correct. Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic, that was 17th to 19 July, 2002. Prosecutor versus Hadzihasanovic and Kubura, over a period of 21 to 31 March, 2005. Prosecutor versus Halilovic, 18 to 22 April, 2005. And of course, Prosecutor versus Dragomir Milosevic, 27 to 29 March, 2007. And I will wait for the interpretation to catch up and you can just tell me if any of those dates are wrong.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no chance of confirming yes or no. I know I was there but I certainly don't remember the date. As soon as I did it every time, I forgot about it. This is my eighth time in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do those dates sound about right, though?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And in each of those trials, as in this trial, you promise to tell the whole truth and nothing but the truth; isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And your memory of events was fresher then than it is now; isn't that true? That is to say, memory of events from 1993 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your memory of events from 1993 to 1995 was fresher when you testified in these other trials than it is today.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a question you could argue about. I cannot remember some events even from 1995, but if you show me a document, it jogs my memory, and the same applies to more recent times. Documents are very important, they jog the memory. Many details are forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So you remember more about 1993 to 1995 now in 2008 than you did in 2002, for instance, when you testified in Galic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I'm saying that I can recall many facts even today if I see a document that reminds me of an event or an important fact, but without documents, I have no memory at all. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, we can move on to some documents, then. You've also given statements to the Prosecutor on three different occasions; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's closer to 13 than three.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, I'll focus on just three for the purposes of this examination. Specifically, these have been loaded into e-court so we can show them to you if you want, but you gave statements to the Prosecutor in 2000, 2001, and 2003. Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave statements beginning with 1999, when I returned from the United States, successively until perhaps two years ago when they let me breathe a little. I went to Nedzarici almost every week to give statements. I cannot remember every statement. I gave many of them. Some of them I signed, others I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You signed three statements. I can show you those if you like, General. Perhaps that would be best. If we could bring P06280 on the screen and if we could stay on page 1 at first. Now, sir, do you see that on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If we could scroll down to the bottom of that page, at least in the English version. And that is your signature at the bottom, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the English version, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, if we could see P06281. And if we could please scroll to the bottom of the English version. This is your signature again, isn't it, General Karavelic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And there's just one more. Could we see P06282. And again, this is your signature at the bottom of the English version, isn't it, General Karavelic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, but I wonder, is there a signature on the Bosnian version?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Let's move to page 5 of this document, that is page 5 in English, at least. Now, that's your signature again, isn't it, General Karavelic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And if we could scroll up in the English version. Now, what it says there is: "This statement has been read over to me in the Bosnian language and is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection. I have given this statement voluntarily and I am aware that it may be used in legal proceedings before the International Criminal Tribunal for the Prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international law in the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991. And that I may be called to give evidence in public before the Tribunal." So that was read to you and you signed at the bottom of that; isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: We can put this document away for now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, General Karavelic, I want to ask you some questions about your experience as the 1st Corps Commander. Now, it's true, isn't it, that as the Commander of the 1st Corps, you were consumed with the defence of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: For example, in Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic, a question was put to you by the Judges, this was on 22 April, 2005 at page 71, lines 16 to 22: "You were very busy for every minute that you were awake trying to defend Sarajevo and also your area of responsibility outside Sarajevo on the other side of the tunnel on Igman; is that correct?" And your answer to that was: "Absolutely." Do you stand by that answer today, sir?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't hear the last part of your question very well, the one where Igman was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'll repeat it, sir, and again I'm reading straight from the transcript here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The question was put to you by the Trial Chamber: "You were very busy for every minute that you were awake trying to defend Sarajevo and also your area ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting my learned friend but I cannot follow what he's talking about since on his exhibit list, there are three statements that have been shown recently to the witness. But this transcript that he is invoking now is not on the list, therefore I cannot see it, follow it, or check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, it's not on the exhibit list, that's true, Your Honour, but this is a public proceeding of the Trial Chamber in Halilovic. There are other cases in which he has testified. I believe it is proper and acceptable to put what the witness has said to him as things that he said in other proceedings before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That is correct, but I also think that parties are under an obligation to inform each other of the documents that they intend to bring up during their examination, either in chief or cross. Please refresh my memory and tell me again which trial you are quoting the witness from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: This is from the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic, 22 April, 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, is it possible for you to draw it up on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. On many occasions we ran into situations like this and we always notified the Prosecutor about which statement we will be using, not only to be able to see that part but rather to have the context of things to be able to check what the witness is talking about there, and the context of the statement in general. I cannot accept the Prosecutor putting forth a small passage of a statement that I cannot check. They should have put it on list, that's why they exist. They included the three statements just shown to the witness, but not this one. I see no reason for not doing so. I simply cannot follow what the Prosecutor is saying and I cannot check the context that the witness was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. That was the point that I was trying to make just a while ago is I think that it is most conducive to the speedy and successful evolvement of the proceedings if both parties are informed of the documents that the other party intends to use during the examination. Mr. Wood, do you have an important reason for wanting to bring up this quotation because if not, then I suggest you move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The point is, Your Honour, to show that the witness was very, very busy defending the city of Sarajevo. I can quote from another -- one of the statements that is on the Exhibit list, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can't you just take his testimony for him to have to prove it? Why don't you just ask that question to the witness, get his answer and then let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm interested in speeding the process along as quickly as I can as well. I just wanted to add some context to that, some facts to back that up. With Mr. President's indulgence, I'll ask just a few questions along this line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, but I think it's -- I think we should leave the old testimony from Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: In your 2001 statement, General Karavelic, P06281 at page 8, you said: "The corps headquarters functioned 24 hours a day, every day." That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And you said that the corps commander was briefed at 8.00 in the operations room and then again at 8.00 p.m. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evenings, it would be the corps commander who would usually brief, but in the morning at 8.00, the commander wasn't always there, perhaps the Chief of Staff was but more or less what you said is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: It's fair to say that you spent every waking moment in your job to defend the city of Sarajevo; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, one could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And this often required you to be outside the city of Sarajevo, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, you had about 70.000 soldiers in the 1st Corps; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even up to 80.000 in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And only about 40.000, 43.000 of those were actually in the city of Sarajevo, the rest were outside the city in your area of responsibility; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a bit less in the city of Sarajevo itself, but around that number, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: For example, you told us on Tuesday on page 47, line 6 that you were on Mount Igman on 30 July 1993 when you sent what has been marked Exhibit 1247 [Realtime transcript read in error "1427"].

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I see in the transcript that it says Exhibit 1427 what I meant to say is 1247, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, with these responsibilities, it wasn't part of your regular duties to attend meetings of the General Staff or the SVK, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My duty was to attend meetings at the General Staff when summoned [Realtime transcript read in error "someone"] by the commander of the General Staff. As for any and all other meetings held by the commander of the General Staff on other issues, it was up to him who would be present at what meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Just so we're clear, sir, until 1995, you were not a part of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The 1st Corps headquarters was not in the same building as the Supreme Command staff, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And that the 1st Corps headquarters was not in the same building as General Delic's office; that's true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we still have it on the screen, there is something incorrect in the transcript. It is page 21, line 7. Perhaps my learned friend could repeat the question from lines 4 and 5. What was discussed is whether the witness was or was not present at the meetings of the General Staff. What we have on the transcript is imprecise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I don't know. I think it's clear enough. What is the question ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, instead of "someone" it should be "summoned." I know what the witness said. He didn't say someone, he said summoned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think these are the kinds of errors that will be corrected in the review of the transcripts. This is an obvious linguistic thing that everyone can see it's an error and it will be corrected ultimately. Please proceed, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. President, I believe I heard the witness say "summoned" as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, General Karavelic, as such a busy 1st Corps Commander, you didn't even have daily contact with General Delic; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Literally speaking, there was no daily contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, General, as 1st Corps Commander, you were never a member of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And it follows from that that it was never part of your duty to attend Presidency meetings?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps on one or two occasions, I wasn't present at Presidency meetings when General Delic was away in 1994 or 1995; however, I'm not certain of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You weren't present at the Presidency meeting on the 8th of June 1993, for example?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And you testified that you didn't see General Delic until later that evening so you don't know what he was doing earlier in the day, do you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he did on that day but I do know what he was doing before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And it follows from all of this, General Karavelic, that you did not attend the Presidency sessions in which the question of the 9th and 10th Brigades was raised?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I was or was not there on one or two occasions on behalf of General Delic, however, I truly cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I see Mr. President that it's about 3.30. This is a place where I could make a convenient break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: All right, because we are 15 minutes shorter today because of the delayed beginning of the hearings so we can either take those 15 minutes now or we can continue for another 15 minutes but that's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I would also be happy to continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So if you are ready to continue, let's carry on until 3.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So it follows from this, General Karavelic, that you don't know firsthand what Rasim Delic said or did during the Presidency discussions relating to Caco and Celo?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What session do you have in mind, the 8th of June? Are you making the link between that session and Caco and Celo? I'm afraid I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm sorry for that confusion, General. I'll put it to you more simply. You were not present at any Presidency sessions in which the issue of Caco and Celo was raised.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said a moment ago, I believe it might be possible that I attended one or two sessions on behalf of General Delic, however, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your answer says and I quote, "I attended one or two sessions on behalf of General Delic." That would suggest that when you were present, General Delic was not present; is that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, as to the Presidency, you've told us earlier today that one member of the Presidency was Mirko Pejanovic. Can you tell us who were the other members of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Wood, this is -- and I hope I'm not wrong, I think this is a misrepresentation of what the witness told us. My recollection is that in a Mirko Pejanovic was presiding the Council For Protection of the Constitutional Order, but I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Was Mirko Pejanovic a member of the Presidency, sir?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was. Mirko Pejanovic was a member of the Presidency of the Bosnia-Herzegovina and also a member of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If you can recall, sir, who were the other members of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to Mirko Pejanovic, on the Serbian side, there was Mrs. Tatjana Ljujic-Mijatovic. On behalf of the Croatian people there was Mr. Kljujic and Komsic. And on behalf of the Bosniaks, there was Alija Izetbegovic, Nijaz Durakovic and Ejup Ganic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, sir, that under the constitution, General Delic was also a member of the Presidency during the time of war?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now of those people that you named, sir, including General Delic, which of these people had any military experience or training?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think I can tell you anything about it. I don't know anything about their past as regards that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: But you do know that General Delic had quite extensive military training, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, when you were appointed to the Supreme Command staff, that was in August of 1995, you told us. It's a fact, sir, isn't it, that you were almost immediately sent to Novi Travnik to take up your duties there to prepare the joint combat with the HV, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does it mean immediately? I went in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And before that, you engaged in discussions, high-level discussions with the Croats, that is the Croatian government, in coming up with plans for joint combat; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So even though you were head of operations and planning, you were actually doing a more important task which is discussing things with higher level commands?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the commanders from the Republic of Croatia, then the answer is yes. As for the commanders of my army, well, that was something normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your function as chief of the division of operations and planning was mostly to coordinate the forces in the 5th and 7th Corps in western Bosnia; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By virtue of an order, I was appointed to a new temporary duty. That was called command for western Bosnia, and I did what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And between the time you were appointed, that is in August 19th, and the time you were sent to Novi Travnik, you didn't really engage in day-to-day, in the job of chief of operations and planning, that is to say, your job was a more important one, discussions with the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operational division or administration on average comprised 60 to 70 officers. I headed it. When I was temporarily assigned to the new temporary duty, of course I had the additional task and I was working on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, sir, you spoke a little bit about the 3rd Corps in response to some of the questions from the Judges, specifically today at line 12, page 10, you said you "don't see why the 3rd Corps Commander would share his problems with me. I did not share mine with him."

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So you had no firsthand knowledge of what was happening in the 3rd Corps between 1993 and 1995; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And just before the break, I want to ask you a little bit about the documents that we saw yesterday in relation to planning -- I'm sorry, strike that, in relation to training. We saw a number of documents that General Delic had signed mandating certain training, and certain training also took place in 1993, 1994, and 1995; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: We also saw on one of the video clips that was played General Delic was speaking, and this is at Exhibit 1330, if we need to pull this up, Exhibit 1330, minute 1:27 to minute 1:56, he said, "We have an increasingly operational army." Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I respond? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you agree with what General Delic said on that tape, sir?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I failed to notice yesterday that he said that. If indeed did say that, we start from one single fact. If we take any NATO army as being 100 per cent operational and on the other hand, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in early 1992, one might say it was zero per cent operational, we need to know at what exact time General Delic said what he said. If that figure improved by 20 to 30 per cent, then one might say it is true; however, it's still very as far from 100 per cent. This is how I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'll put it to you more plainly. The ABiH did improve over time, didn't it, General Karavelic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: It was a more disciplined and a better army in 1995 than it was in 1993; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And this would be a convenient time for me to take a break, Your Honour, before I launch into something that will take a little bit more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's a good idea. We will break and come back at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wood, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Before we move on to the next topic, there is one thing I want to clear up in the record, General Karavelic. There is an answer that wasn't clear. I asked you at page 26, line 1: "You had no firsthand knowledge of what was happening in the 3rd Corps between 1993 and 1995; isn't that true?" And your answer was, "No." So I just want to put it to you plainly, you had no firsthand knowledge of what was happening in the 3rd Corps between 1993 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What does that mean for you, firsthand?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Okay. For example, you weren't on the 3rd Corps line of communications.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You weren't being sent combat reports by the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You weren't being sent military security reports by the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So your only knowledge of what was happening in the 3rd Corps was as you said earlier, hearsay, secondhand?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I want to talk a little bit about communications now. You told us on the first day at page 34, line 11 and I'll quote: "Communications with units outside of Sarajevo, any kind of communication was scarce. There was no continuity, there were frequent and long breakdowns and the means of communications were very poor." Now, you also told us that same day at page 35, line 23 and I quote: "I can confirm that the commander of the General Staff had very sparse information about the status of the other corps." Do you remember saying those things, General Karavelic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you were not a member of the General Staff in 1993.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So you have no firsthand knowledge of what was -- what information was actually reaching General Delic, do you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could put it that way. But I interpret all that based on my experience of my corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask you a little bit about that then. Now, you told us earlier that about 30.000 of your troops were actually outside the city of Sarajevo. That's true, right?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot vouch for the exact number, but roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: In any event, there was a certain number of soldiers that you had to communicate with who were outside the city. That's the main point; right?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, we know from your testimony that you had at your disposal packet communication. You told us today, for example, that packet communication were available only to the General Staff when communicating with corps commanders and others.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You also told us on the first day of your testimony that, "Thanks to General Delic, on the 31st of July, 1st of August, I received two units from Central Bosnia." You remember saying that too?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And we can -- we know that you were speaking about Exhibit 1247 which was dated the 30th of July, 1993. It would follow from this, sir, wouldn't it, that General Delic did have communication with units in Central Bosnia if he was able to call them and send them to your rescue; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you put something to me and then you want me to say yes or no, and the answer may be who knows what, if you want a real answer. I don't know if I have the right to speak of assumptions as a witness. What if General Delic had no communications with those units? And as far as those units that came to assist me, I can say with absolute certainty that General Delic had no contact with them whatsoever because they are units too small for General Delic to have anything to do with them. Those were just two companies. What if, at the insistence of the commander, the president of the Presidency called on satellite telephone and then a politician was told somewhere in Zenica or in Travnik and then that politician called somebody at a lower level and all that resulted in the arrival of those two units. You simply say he had communication with those two units. That does not hold water.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So there were satellite telephones as well, sir?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's the image I have in my mind, that that's something I heard, that the president of the Presidency had one, but I cannot vouch for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, as for you, you had at your disposal communication via courier as well; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the city of Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, you told us, and this was in relation to Exhibit 1247 when you were speaking about sending a message from outside the city of Sarajevo to the General Staff, what you told the Trial Chamber, and this is at page 47, line 17: "That there were two possible ways of sending information, either by packet communications or by courier." When you gave that answer, you knew that you were talking about communication from outside the city of Sarajevo into the city of Sarajevo, didn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I clarified yesterday how one could cross the runway of the airport until the tunnel was dug. Out of 100 attempts, one was successful. Don't hold me to this number, but I'm telling you this just to illustrate what chances a messenger had in that situation. It was pure lottery, but once in a while he would make it. Whereas the situation on the ground changes from one moment to another. You cannot call that means of communication, but I kind of despair of explaining that to you. A courier, a messenger is the most primitive type of communication today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You had at your disposal, sir, communication via telephone as well; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the city of Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, sir, in your testimony -- I'm sorry, in your statement from 2000, this is P06280, when you're speaking about Operation Neretva, and for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, this was an operation in which certain troops that were under the command and control of General Karavelic were sent outside the city of Sarajevo to participate in an operation in the Neretva river valley. You said in your statement, sir, that "During operation Neretva 1993, I received one report from Adnan Solakovic by courier and we talked on the telephone." Now, it's plain that he was in the Neretva river valley when you had this conversation with him and that you were in the city of Sarajevo and you spoke with him via telephone. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I talked by telephone but I'm not sure with General Halilovic, Sefer Halilovic. And if you recall, since you were involved in the Sefer Halilovic case, there was one letter written in longhand by Adnan Solakovic and I got it that way. And I don't remember talking to Adnan Solakovic and if I did it must have been by radio, open communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: In fact, you spoke to Adnan Solakovic and you also spoke to General Halilovic during the course of Neretva 1993, isn't that true, and that is via radio or telephone?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And it's true that when you spoke with them they were in the Neretva river valley and you were in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Wood, I don't want to interfere in your cross-examination but I am curious to see where we are going with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. This goes to the statement that General Karavelic made about communication between units outside of Sarajevo and units within Sarajevo. He has told us that he has no firsthand knowledge about what information was reaching General Delic. He can only speak of his own experience, of his own experience with communications communicating with troops outside of Sarajevo. These examples that I brought up show that despite what he told us earlier, he did in fact have solid means of communication. He could communicate when he's talking to the Supreme Command by packet communication, he could communicate via radio or telephone and at certain points he could communicate via courier. This shows that -- this completes, I think, the picture of the state of communications between units in Sarajevo where we know General Delic was headquartered and units outside of Sarajevo, for example, where Sefer Halilovic and Adnan Solakovic were in September 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And just how is that relevant to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: We've heard a lot of testimony particularly today, Your Honour, and particularly from this witness about how there was very poor communications between General Delic and his subordinate commands. This - and I don't want to speak for the Defence here - but I believe the Defence theory is that this would tend to affect his ability to command and effectively control his troops. The point of the testimony that I'm eliciting now, Mr. President, is to show that there were means of communication between units inside of Sarajevo where General Delic was most of the time and units outside of Sarajevo through the example of the 1st Corps Commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. I'm hesitating a bit because I don't think that we have been offered testimony to suggest that there was no communication. We have been offered various sources which would suggest that communication was sometimes difficult which, again, is not surprising during war, but -- well, I leave it to you to carry on but I also urge you to focus on the things that you need to elicit with this witness, from this witness in relation to your indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could I have Exhibit 1331 brought up on the screen, please. And for the record this was an exhibit that was entered into evidence through this witness earlier this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, General Karavelic, you see this on the screen?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You saw this earlier this week. I just want to ask you, have you seen this particular document before?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Maybe yes, maybe no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the format of this document?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean am I familiar? I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, have you seen documents like this before? Documents headed this way, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Supreme Command Staff Bulletin.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Did you see documents like this when you were 1st Corps Commander?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how often would you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am very sorry, you saw it or not? Please try to focus and tell us if you have seen something like that or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe yes, maybe no. I received, throughout the war, millions of documents, and you must understand that this is an impossible question. If you want me to say yes just to please someone, I will say yes but I'm trying to speak the truth. If you don't believe me, that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not recall if this document was already shown to you by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I can confirm that it was, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let's see what you have to say, in fact, we'll take your answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I? The Defence did show that document to the witness, but in a completely different context. The Defence focused on the contents, not on these facts and we didn't ask the witness whether he had received the document or not. I just want to make this clear to -- I don't want the witness to seem to be saying something different to what he said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: General Karavelic, did you receive bulletins of this type during the war, that is between 1993 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not 100 per cent sure, but if I had to choose, I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: We can put that document away now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: During your direct examination, General Karavelic, you told us a little bit about Operation Trebevic and I want to ask you a little bit more about this. Now, you told us that you were able to neutralise the 9th and 10th Brigades which then consisted of around 2.000 to 3.000 men; do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And you said you had a force of about 4.500 men to accomplish this task; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And it's true that Rasim Delic personally commanded this?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He commanded together with the Minister of Interior Bakir Alispahic and the team they had with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: It's true also, isn't it, General Karavelic, that an operation like Trebevic is an extraordinary operation for dealing with renegade troops; would that be a correct way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could put it that way, although the matter is much broader and more complex than what you described.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I will get into more specifics then. Now, when an ARBiH commander learns of criminal behaviour on the part of his troops, he has other means at his disposal to discipline them; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the Prosecutor be kind to clarify what he means by "commander of the BiH army because yesterday we mentioned both General Delic in that capacity and the president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm speaking generally of any ARBiH commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no such position, commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Let me put it more simply then. You as 1st Corps Commander, when you learn that your troops are engaging in criminal behaviour, or behaving in disruptive behaviour, in disruptive ways, you can order them to be investigated by competent law enforcement; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You can issue verbal warnings to the troops; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You can even refer them to, if they are serious enough infractions, the military disciplinary court; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just asking how, when I have no access to these soldiers and these commanders? If they saw me, they would have killed me on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm speaking generally, sir. Generally.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You do speak generally a lot, but sometimes you go into detail, specific detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: All right. We'll speak about the criminality of the 9th and 10th then. Now you knew about their criminal acts; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I think your testimony was, sir, that there had been requests to the Supreme Command to do something about the 9th and 10th Brigade starting from before you were 1st Corps Commander in May 1993 and that when you became 1st Corps Commander, you also sought leave to deal with the 9th and 10th Mountain Brigades. That's correct, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. But I did that on the basis of certain indications, clues, not on the basis of absolute knowledge that they had committed a crime at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Certainly you had notice that they were doing something that was wrong.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: It's safe to say, sir, that you did everything you could to make sure this problem was taken care of, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I took the steps that I was required to take in my position and that I was capable of taking in such a difficult, complex situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And it's true, actually, sir, that you took extraordinary steps, didn't you? You went to the president himself and you told him: If you don't take care of this, I will resign my post as 1st Corps Commander.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And you did this because you knew that if these troops continued to commit these crimes in your area of responsibility, that you would be responsible for not taking care of it, didn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, there's been one issue, sir, that has been running through your testimony here. You told us at page 58, line 1 of Tuesday's transcript that Alija Izetbegovic was undermining the war effort. And you repeated this at page 60, line 19. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember the question. When one says that he was undermining and you include that in your question, then you receive such an answer as specific as that. I can say that he did and he did not. If the Commander of the 1st Corp as early as May sent a letter requesting that certain brigade commanders be removed, and if the General Staff was acquainted with it, and if Commander General Delic demanded from the president countless times that that should be approved and done, still, it took five to six months. It was only done on the 26th of October, after certain crimes, and after a number of soldiers were killed in the operation. Then my question would be: What was all of that? I would say that it was undermining and was not at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Of course you don't know exactly that General Delic demanded from the president countless times that something should be done. You don't know that, do you, sir?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many times, but I do know that he was requesting it. He was supporting me in my requests, and he would tell me exert pressure on the president and he was doing the same. I'm not merely saying this for the sake of telling you just anything, but that's how things were. It would not have happened had General Delic had a different opinion. It would not have been done without him, even if the president had ordered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Of course, the topic of this indictment is the El Mujahid Detachment, you know that, sir, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know of it to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And it seems as though maybe the implication, perhaps, is that a comparison was to be drawn, would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean specifically. If you can be more concrete, I can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: General Karavelic, did Alija Izetbegovic prevent Rasim Delic from taking action against the El Mujahid Detachment, is that what you're trying to tell us?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My testimony is that he prevented me from dealing with my renegade commanders and soldiers. You can draw a parallel that he may have been doing the same thing with the other issue but I can neither confirm nor deny it. I was outside that story. General Delic is the only person who can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So the crimes and the misdeeds of the 9th and 10th Brigade between May 1993 and October 1993, those are the fault of Alija Izetbegovic because he didn't do anything to crack down on these troops?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alija Izetbegovic passed away. I don't want to be so specific in my answer if as early as May, before I became the corps commander, my corps commander kept insisting that such brigade commanders be removed. Then I thought that when Sefer Halilovic was still the head of the army, that he was the obstacle but when Rasim Delic came, I became convinced that we shared the same position, that is, I and my Commander General Delic, however, Izetbegovic still wouldn't do what we were asking for. When we finally confronted him with the information on the crimes that had been committed, and the very same brigade commander used mortars to fire at his own command and Presidency, it was only then that the president consented. If you're asking me, I would say that General Delic had similar problems in his relation to the Mujahedin and in relation to dealing with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You're just speculating now, sir, isn't that true? You don't know anything about relations between General Delic and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not included in all that. I was present at certain meetings of commanders --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first and foremost, you will recall that a few moments ago, the Prosecutor invited the witness to draw a parallel between what was taking place and whether or not Mr. Izetbegovic prevented General Delic and now when the witness answered, the Prosecutor is saying that he's speculating. Your Honours, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Wood, I am on Madam Vidovic's side in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get to the heart of exactly of what General Karavelic is trying to suggest and what the Defence is trying to suggest by putting on the evidence of Trebevic 2 which is not actually relevant to the indictment, Your Honour. It's not a crime that's been charged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm fully aware of it. I thought your question regarding Mujahedin was quite bold but I think the witness gave a reasonable answer. So take what you can from that and proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. And I think on that note, the Prosecution has no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, but a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, General Karavelic, to go back to the briefings that you mentioned. Her Honour asked you about whether you were present at the meetings at which corps commanders briefed on the various problems; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you about you as the corps commander. What did you inform them during those briefings? What sort of problems and what sort of command levels did you brief on?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I briefed them on the current combat situation within my area of responsibility, i.e., where my defence lines were stable and weak, where I was expecting the aggressor to attack and so on and so forth. That was number one. Number two, there was another important issue that persisted throughout the war and that was discipline and internal organisation, in other words, the chain of command. The first issue of the briefing depended very much on the second issue, that is the ability to execute a task. This was discussed openly. Given the conditions that we had to wage war under and at the same time we were very transparent in our work, well, I would say that even the most modern armies should envy us on that concerning combat morale and logistics, whether there was food or not, whether there was ammunition or not, where we can get it from, how it should be bought, do we buy it from the aggressor, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. All those issues are raised, the commander makes conclusions and we set out tasks and then we go about implementing them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The purpose of my question was the following: Was there any discussion of small-scale units the size of platoons or detachments or did you only discuss general problems?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed various and different units. We saw a document yesterday ordering that certain units be assigned to different corps. There was discussion about indiscipline, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I only have a few questions concerning the 9th and 10th Brigades or rather, not so much the brigades but the issues of procedure that you used. You were asked by the Prosecutor whether you could initiate an investigation. Is it a duty of a corps commander or of his command whenever they heard of a crime to initiate an investigation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I could correct you where you say "whenever they heard." I would say that whenever we get by official information that there was serious crimes that had been committed and serious violations of the law, then it was a duty of a corps commander to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that as the corps commander, you did get by certain indications of crimes committed and you said you reported that as well as Commander Delic did. Did the Presidency ask for any proof or did they just take your word for it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did ask for proof.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you do anything about it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. My office began collecting information. It lasted for a while, and perhaps in September or October, we compiled the information and forwarded it and after that, the thing we discussed happened. Lastly, decisions were made to initiate proceedings, and people were charged with war crimes, 30 or 40 of them, and many more were charged with infractions and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. As the corps commander at the time, did you or did you not have to prove that you used proportionate force to the events? When I say proportionate, did you have to convince the Presidency that you used proportionate force?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could say yes to that, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the use of force, does one always have to prove the proportionality of the force used to the events in the field?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has to be proven --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is the last in a series of leading questions. This is a redirect, it's not a cross-examination. The questions cannot be leading on redirect. I object on this ground, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sustained. Madam Vidovic, please rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In what situations is force used? When?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think a day or two, I gave you an answer concerning that question. In cases of serious or large-scale war crimes, or when there is a large number of incidents in which violations of law and regulations occur.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
