utterances.text: What about the evidence concerning those? Were you supposed to present that to the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Judge Lattanzi?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I would like to address the matter which was raised by Mr. Wood in his cross-examination because the matter that he brought up is obviously at the heart of this case. I think Mr. Wood suggested the question of why would General Delic and President Izetbegovic go to such extreme measures to bring the 9th and the 10th Brigades in your corps to order if similar steps were not taken to bring other independent and insubordinate groups within the jurisdiction of the ABiH. I'm not sure that you are in a position to provide much evidence to that question, but I would like to ask you if you have an opinion about the reasons that might have been underlying the way in which the 9th and the 10th Brigades in your corps were treated differently from other insubordinate parts of the ABiH. Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or rather why President Izetbegovic had not made that decision earlier. I believe that is the gist of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I must have expressed myself badly. I'm asking you if you have an opinion about why steps similar to those which were taken to bring the 9th and the 10th Brigade under control were not taken in respect of other insubordinate groups which we have heard in this trial were posing problems in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, undertaking the steps such as those taken in Sarajevo itself against the 9th and the 10th Brigade stands as a commander and a senior officer at the time, I was trying to understand on one side the president of the Presidency, since he was the most responsible person for all military and political affairs in relation to Bosnia-Herzegovina and its defence. I'm not trying to defend his position. I said what I said here. However, he did have a significant dilemma before him. On one side, he knew that those commanders and their soldiers were committing serious infractions and even war crimes. On the other hand, given the situation that the city was in, as well as the rest of the country, the support those people enjoyed among the population was one of the key factors. I suppose that President Izetbegovic inter alia waited all that time with his approval for an armed operation against Caco and Celo for the following reasons: Firstly, to have 100 per cent certain arguments to go about doing that. And secondly, to have enough time to politically prepare the context and the situation. He wanted the citizens on his side and for them to be ready to discard of those commanders since they were posing as heros, as the best and most courageous commanders. It was for that reason, I presume, that the president was dragging his feet. He wanted the civilian population on his side so that once the armed force is used, as few as possible civilians would be hurt. We can discuss that part, and this is my opinion. The Mujahedin were a completely different issue. I don't want to go into it right now. However, if you will ask me to, then I will do so. These commanders were there. We knew where they were, their address, their building, their office. We knew where the soldiers supporting them were. It was far easier for me to do it. On top of that, as I said, most of the population was on our side by that time and they agreed with an armed operation aimed at those people. From my channels of information and throughout the war, I knew what the Mujahedin issue was, in particular, in relation to the Mujahedin and Kubura case, they had a lot of population on their side, they provided them with humanitarian assistance, clothes and so on and so forth, and that was their main achievement. That is why they did not see an operation against for such a long time. I am familiar -- I was familiar with the situation to a large extent and given all the information I had, I believe that doing that earlier would have been impossible and they were also very dispersed from Zepce to Bugojno which is a distance of 300 to 400 kilometres and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems as if you are saying that some action was taken against the Mujahedin; is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know some of the things I know because I studied documents in preparing an expert report in the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case, and I can only discuss this issue through the documents I studied at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of your report in that other case, but my question to you in this case was were you aware of any action which was finally taken to bring the Mujahedin under control by General Delic or by President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, measures were taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Which measures?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, as far as I remember one particular document, General Delic ordered the 3rd Corps Commander to disarm, disband, and even expel them. But if you remember my previous answer, that was impossible to do, and then there were other documents about establishing detachments, et cetera, and from all these documents it transpires that General Delic was always of the opinion that the Mujahedin bring only harm and very little -- and are of very little use and that they should be done with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I would like to know something, but only if you know. From what you've learnt during the conflict, is this something that you knew at the time or what you know now, what you're telling us now, is this something that you found out while you were preparing yourself to testify as an expert witness in the Hadzihasanovic case?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know most of what I know from preparing the expert report in Hadzihasanovic, and I also know some things because I was involved in the war from beginning to end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That is something that I had not understood when you answered my question, but thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: General, do you know if General Delic considered to follow-up on his order to disarm the Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assure you as a human being, and as an officer, that he did. It's quite another matter whether he was in a position to, whether he received or could have received an approval from the president of the Presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic to use force or something similar. Of his own accord, he did not have the right to do any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What, to your knowledge, could have prevented General Delic from following up on the order that he gave to have the Mujahedin Detachment disarmed and disbanded? I mean I assume that once he had issued that order, he would also be in a position to follow up on it in case no action was taken. And my question to you, therefore, is: Do you know if he considered that? And you're telling me yes, he did. My next question, therefore, is: What prevented him from doing that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, there are several reasons but I'll state only one. I'm deeply convinced that he considered and took those steps, but when the Mujahedin arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina, they immediately scattered themselves across various villages in Central Bosnia. They were never in one single base or location, unlike our units. They very quickly found wives among the local population, started families. They had all the support of the local population in terms of food and clothing because it was very difficult to survive at that time. Any attempt that General Delic took on his own to disarm them would inevitably have led to loss of life among civilians. He did not have the right to do that without approval from the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: When you tell us that in General Delic's view, the Mujahedin Detachment was more of a nuisance than they actually did any good, what sort of nuisance are we talking about? Can you give us examples of the irregularities that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I'm going to say is my opinion. I wouldn't like to go into it really, but since you ask. There are many reasons, again. Here is one. Those people who came from outside, they started observing their religion in their own way that was particular to them. One part of the local Muslim population accepted that. If a Mujahedin married a local girl, it was almost automatic. On the other hand, I know in Sarajevo, a large portion of the Muslim population was against them. They were saying, "What do we need them for? They only cause problems and they bring confusion in our religion." That was one of the reasons for opposition. There were others, of course. Later, there were rumours that they had committed war crimes and we know very well how we treated war crimes in our army. You have the example of our own men, Caco and Celo. It is therefore my personal opinion that they brought us much more trouble and shame than any benefit. Unfortunately, nobody asked my opinion or General Delic's. I am telling you this as a human being sitting in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Fair enough. I'm insisting a bit on this because it is important to our understanding of the facts of this case. You tell us that in reply to my answer about what the problems with the Mujahedin, you tell us that there were two problems, that there were religious problems and should I say cultural or social problems in the communities in which they resided and there were also rumours of war crimes. So these were the two problems that General Delic would have faced. The rumours about war crimes, how were they -- how did you learn about that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, Your Honour, it took me a long time to get any facts about the war crimes committed by Caco. He started committing them in the end of 1992 and beginning of 1993, whereas I was only able to present what I found out to my superiors in October 1993. Whereas in those areas where they were, unlike those units that were in my area under my command, it's very difficult to prove a war crime. I'm just proceeding from the knowledge that no axis was possible there. Nobody could come close to the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see. But how did you learn about the war crimes? You told us that there were rumours about war crimes and my question is how did you learn about that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never learned anything for certain. I cannot tell you anything with any certainty now. All I knew was what I saw on television and stories that circulated around town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's exactly what I was looking for. How did you hear about the rumours of war crimes committed by the Mujahedin fighters? So you just told me now that it was the talk of the town and there was television reports, and did you hear of war crimes from others?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you discuss these rumours with your fellow corps commanders?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say either that I did or that I didn't. I probably did, but that conversation ends in nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: General, officially or unofficially, what I am curious to know is if the rumours of war crimes committed by the foreign Arab fighters in Bosnia also reached the inner circles of the leadership of the ABiH, that is to say, the corps commanders and the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I talk about this, I primarily mean the end of the war, and the transition period towards peace after the Dayton Accords. In 1993, I never heard anything so it's difficult for me to give a precise answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I thank you very much. Do any of the parties have any questions arising out of questions from the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, General, can you be more precise? When did you hear those rumours, at the time of the war, after the war?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said towards the end of the war at the time when we were already moving towards peace.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you discuss those rumours with General Delic ever?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you heard rumours about town and stories about the Mujahedin on television, when did these programmes start appearing on television?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of the war. It's difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These stories, did they concentrate on one specific group or Arabs generally in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour, that's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I would agree. Can you rephrase, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all due respect, I gave the witness two options, but never mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, forget what I said before. Tell me, who did these stories concern? Someone specific or not?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one specific. It was a general story speaking of some Arabs, some Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question, General Karavelic. For three days now, you have been giving evidence saying that you, as corps commander, requested the use of force. Have you ever heard of any other corps commander doing the same, requesting the use of force for similar purposes?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was it or was it not necessary for the corps commander to request use of force for the matter to be considered at all?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've said this more than once, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you have to corroborate your request with facts?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic. Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: There is some difficulty, Your Honour. When I'm waiting for the translation, often times it's hard to object because the answer has already been given by the time the offending question has been asked. I would just note that the last question, "Would you have to corroborate your request with facts," is again a leading question. And I would suggest even though I didn't have the time to object to that, that whatever answer he gives to leading questions like this should be given very little weight. With that said, Your Honour, I do have some questions to ask him specifically in regards to his expert report in Hadzihasanovic since that has come up before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: General Karavelic, you did say that you prepared an expert report for the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Wood, sorry, because I'm wary of the time. If you have a number of questions that you wish to put then I suggest we take the break now and reconvene at 6.00. The alternative would be to ask you if you intend or if you -- yes, intend to finish before quarter to 6.00. In that case, I would be willing to go on until quarter to 6.00 and then we can close. But if you need more time, that's perfectly all right, then we'll just adjourn now and reconvene at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I think I can finish by a quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's good, Mr. Wood. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let us just clear up one matter, just one, please. General Vahid Karavelic is testifying here and testified in examination in chief as a fact witness and not as an expert. The Court of course has the right to ask any question at all and you did so, Your Honour, but I do oppose any attempt by the Prosecutor to ask questions that fall in the domain of expertise. Here, he appears as a fact witness concerning events that we have been discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, I fully agree with you in the sense that it is clear that General Karavelic is not called here as an expert, this is beyond question. If you recall our procedural guidelines, I think in paragraph 6, there is a provision that allows a party to confront a witness with his earlier statements in order to refresh the witness's memory and I was under -- I was under the impression that this is what Mr. Wood is doing. That he wants to confront the witness with something in that report in order to refresh the witness's memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Under those circumstances, my learned friend, Mr. Wood, should have notified us that he would be using the expert report and put it back on the list so that I could review it and have it in mind. The expert report was not listed among the things that would be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm not with you on this one, Madam Vidovic. Documents that are going to be used will have to be disclosed to the other party within the time limits that we have set out. That is one thing. Another thing is to use a document briefly, not to have it introduced into evidence but to only refresh the witness's memory, and for that purpose you do not need, and in most cases you probably can't, disclose, in advance, those documents. So I think it's perfectly legitimate for a party to use a document not for the purpose of admission into evidence but only for the purpose of refreshing the witness's memory and that does not require previous disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to intervene on this also. Mr. Prosecutor, you have the intention to refresh the memory of the witness with this expert report? You intend to put the expert report in the Hadzihasanovic case? And the Halilovic case?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: It was an expert report for the case of Hadzihasanovic and Kubura, just for the record. It's not my intention to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, but I'm against this. This was an expert report and I believe that this cannot be done because there, there are opinions which are expressed, while here, the witness is here a witness -- I think one shouldn't refresh the memory of a witness of facts by a report, an expert report. Therefore, I don't know what to do now ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That settles the matter because the Chamber will then have to prevent you from bringing this report up at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I could clarify. It was not my intention to put the document itself to General Karavelic. I read the report as did Madam Vidovic, but it is not my intention to put it to him to refresh his recollection or anything like that. What I can tell you, the point of asking questions about that is General Karavelic said that a lot of his knowledge with regard to the Mujahedin springs from the research that he did in regards to drafting that expert report. I think it's important for a few -- for the Trial Chamber to bear in mind a few important facts about the scope of that report and about the methodology that went about -- that was used in drafting that. I think now, the impression is that he has an undue amount of expertise about the Mujahedin from 1993 to 1995 when I can tell you, Your Honour, as is on the record, the Hadzihasanovic case, dealt with Hadzihasanovic who was the 3rd Corps Commander only until November 1st, 1993. Therefore I think it's important to elicit from this witness to explain to the Trial Chamber that he has no knowledge, that the scope of his knowledge is specific just to that, to whatever he looked at for the purposes of the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case which went no further than 1 November 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I must say that you are not providing a very correct picture of what General Karavelic has testified here. As far as I recall from the witness's testimony, he has told us that there were rumours about war crimes and that's about it. We have not heard what these war crimes were and we are not in any doubt as to how he learned about these things. So the sources of the rumours also were clear. I don't think that there is any reason to go into the expert report of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Another point that the Prosecution thinks is important to raise is he did mention that there were some measures that General Delic tried to take against the El Mujahid Detachment and I've located exactly what document that is. He's made reference to it. I think it's important, given this, that other questions be put to General Karavelic so that we can understand exactly what his scope of knowledge is to be able to say measures were taken against the Mujahedin by General Delic. As you know, this is at the heart of the matter, the Prosecution believes it's important to be able to follow this up and add context to what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. General Karavelic spoke here about the Mujahedin. I don't remember, and you will correct me if I am wrong, that he ever mentioned measures taken against the detachment called El Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, but on this corps, I would like to add that when the witness expresses opinions, because he also expressed some opinions and the Chamber won't take them on board because he is a witness of fact. So the Trial Chamber can easily make the difference between opinions expressed during his testimony yesterday, today, and facts. But when I asked him, I said you're saying this on the basis of the expert report or on the basis of what you heard during the war, he answered that he had heard something on the basis of the report, the expert report, but certain things he had also learned during the war. Therefore, I think that we have all the elements at hand in order to distinguish, make the difference between what he told us as a witness of a fact during this period, during those events during the war, and what he may have learned later in the light of his testimony in other cases. Therefore, I believe that in order to pacify the parties, the Chamber needs to see -- is quite in a position to see clearly this witness in his deposition, I don't think one should go -- follow this avenue. But I will defer to what the President Judge decides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Wood --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Presiding Judge decides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- I note the time, and wish to know if you insist on going on along this track or whether you have other questions that you wish to put to the witness in response to the answers given by the witness to the questions posed by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution takes heart in what Judge Lattanzi just said about the Trial Chamber's ability to distinguish between what the witness says as a fact witness and what he says as an opinion. I would hope that they apply this to the entirety of his testimony not just to what has transpired in the last few minutes here. And given that, the Prosecution does not believe that it does need to pursue this any further as long as it's understood that what the witness is saying about this is his opinion only, and not facts that he's aware of firsthand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: This is clearly understood by the Chamber. If the parties have no more questions to put, then I think we have reached the end of your testimony and it is incumbent upon me, General, to thank you warmly for having come yet once again to The Hague to offer your testimony and your knowledge about these cases. So I thank you for coming. I thank you for testifying and I wish you a good travel back to your country. Thank you very much. You may leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you recall the situation that we discussed a few days ago, the situation that we had to face because of the difficulties with these Italian documents, we had planned General Cuskic for tomorrow but we had moved him to some point in the future until we found out what is going to happen with the Italian documents and we were unable to predict how long this testimony would take and we were not able to get a witness who was able to come only for a short time because we are not going to sit for a long time, the witness would have to go here and -- to come here and go back. We are not sitting in the next five days, so we would probably have to wait for the Wednesday that follows. That's why I don't have a witness for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. The registrar informs me that the next hearing would be on Thursday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. In that case, I can adjourn for today and say that we will reconvene on Thursday, the 3rd of April at 9.00 a.m. in this courtroom. Mr. Wood, do you have anything to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm just standing up early in honour of Your Judge's departure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's very good of you. You can't wait to see us out of here, I suppose. I wish you all a pleasant time until we meet again. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, April 3, 2008 at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.50 p.m.,
